body:
# Knossos Palace From Heraklion: Bus, Tour or Taxi?

**Short answer:** take the city bus if you simply want to get from central Heraklion to Knossos cheaply.

Take a taxi if you value door-to-door convenience or are travelling as a small group.

Book a tour if what you really want is **a guide, the Archaeological Museum, hotel pickup or a larger Crete itinerary**.

Knossos is only a few kilometres from Heraklion.

You do not need an organized excursion just to reach it.

## Knossos is much closer to Heraklion than many visitors expect

The official Hellenic Heritage site gives the travel time as approximately:

**20 minutes by city bus**

or

**15 minutes by car.**

The archaeological site sits just outside Heraklion, not in some remote corner of Crete.

That changes the decision completely.

If you are already staying in central Heraklion, transport is the easy part.

The more important question is:

**Do you want somebody to explain Knossos when you arrive?**

## The city bus is the default choice for most independent travellers

Heraklion Urban Bus runs **Line 2** between the port area and Knossos.

The route operates every day.

Current schedules show frequent departures through much of the day, and the official archaeological site itself recommends the city bus as one of the normal ways to reach Knossos.

The journey is roughly 20 minutes.

That makes this one of those rare famous archaeological sites where public transport is genuinely simple.

## How much does the bus cost?

Heraklion's urban bus system uses fare zones.

From central Heraklion toward Knossos you cross from Zone A into Zone B.

The current regular fare for an A-to-B journey is:

**€1.80 when bought before boarding**

or

**€2.80 when bought on the bus.**

There is also a €5 day ticket and a €6 24-hour ticket.

Tickets can be bought through the Heraklion Urban Bus app and at authorised sales points.

So for one adult travelling independently, the transport cost can be almost trivial compared with the €20 archaeological-site ticket.

## The bus is best if…

I would take Line 2 if:

* I am staying in central Heraklion
* I am comfortable using public transport
* I want to keep costs down
* I want to arrive early
* I want to decide how long to stay
* I do not need hotel pickup
* I plan to explore the site independently

For a solo traveller or couple in Heraklion city, this is probably the option I would check first.

## Taxi is mainly about convenience

A taxi takes roughly 15 minutes from central Heraklion under normal conditions.

That is only a few minutes faster than the bus.

So speed alone is not a strong reason to choose it.

The useful part is door-to-door travel.

A taxi makes more sense if:

* you have limited walking stamina
* you are travelling with children
* you want to arrive exactly at opening time
* you are carrying bags
* your hotel is awkward for Line 2
* three or four people can split the fare

I could not verify a single official fixed Heraklion–Knossos taxi fare for 2026, so I would not build the decision around a quoted internet price.

Ask for the expected fare before leaving or use a metered/licensed taxi.

## Taxi is not the same as a tour

This distinction sounds obvious, but booking sites often blur it.

A taxi gets you to Knossos.

That is all.

You still need:

* your admission ticket
* your own interpretation
* a guide if you want one
* transport back

If your reason for paying more is to **understand the palace**, spending that money on a guide may deliver much more value than spending it on a more comfortable ride.

## The official Knossos ticket is €20

The official full-price admission is currently **€20**.

Reduced admission is **€10** for qualifying visitors.

The site is open year-round, with longer hours in summer.

From November through March, current winter hours are **08:00–17:00**.

You can buy tickets through the official Hellenic Heritage system.

That €20 admission is important when comparing tours because some tours include it and others do not.

A €50 tour with a ticket included is not necessarily more expensive than a €35 tour that charges €20 admission separately.

## How long do you actually need at Knossos?

Around **1.5 to 2 hours** is realistic for most visitors.

Discover Greece gives roughly 1 hour 30 minutes as enough for a standard visit, with longer needed if you want to explore more thoroughly.

That means Knossos does not require a full day.

From Heraklion, you can reasonably do:

**bus → Knossos → return → lunch → Archaeological Museum**

without turning the whole day into an excursion.

For many people, that is the smartest plan.

## The real reason to pay for a tour: Knossos is difficult to read alone

Knossos is unusual.

Some of what you see is ancient.

Some was heavily reconstructed under archaeologist Arthur Evans in the early 20th century.

The famous red columns and reconstructed rooms are visually memorable, but without context it can be difficult to understand:

* what is original
* what is reconstruction
* what scholars know
* what Evans interpreted
* where the famous frescoes actually are
* how the palace functioned

That is where a good licensed guide earns their money.

## My choice for independent transport + guided visit

One current small-group option lasts about **1 hour 30 minutes**, includes the €20 Knossos admission ticket and uses a licensed guide.

The group is limited to around 16 people.

Transport is **not included**.

That is actually useful rather than a disadvantage if you are staying in Heraklion.

Take the €1.80 bus yourself.

Meet the guide at Knossos.

Pay for expertise instead of paying someone to drive you six kilometres.



[Palace of Knossos Small Group VIP Tour](https://www.viator.com/tours/Crete/Palace-of-Knossos-Tour-small-group/d960-390350P1?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

For many first-time visitors, this combination may be the sweet spot:

**cheap bus + good guide.**

## What about “skip the line”?

Be precise with this phrase.

The small-group tour above includes a **skip-the-ticket-line service**.

That means you avoid having to queue at the ticket counter because admission is already arranged.

It does not mean the archaeological site becomes empty.

You may still encounter crowds at popular reconstructed areas and narrow viewing points.

The useful benefit is convenience.

Not magical private access.

## The Archaeological Museum changes the decision

If you are genuinely interested in Minoan Crete, I would strongly consider combining Knossos with the **Heraklion Archaeological Museum**.

This is where many of the important original finds from Knossos are displayed.

The famous frescoes you associate with Knossos are not simply sitting exposed on palace walls.

Many originals are in the museum.

That means:

**Knossos gives you the place.**

**The museum gives you many of the objects.**

Together they make far more sense.

## If you want Knossos + Museum without logistics

This is where a private or organized tour begins to earn its price.

One current private Heraklion tour combines:

* Knossos
* professional guide
* private air-conditioned transport
* optional Archaeological Museum
* pickup and drop-off

The Knossos admission and museum admission are currently charged separately.



[Private Tour to Knossos and Archaeological Museum or Shopping from Heraklion](https://www.viator.com/tours/Heraklion/Heraklion-tour-to-Knossos-and-Archaeological-Museum-or-Shopping/d961-5389P34?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

I would consider this if:

* you want a deeper history day
* you are travelling as a family or small group
* you dislike coordinating buses and museum tickets
* you are arriving on a cruise ship
* convenience matters more than price

For one independent traveller staying near central Heraklion, it is probably unnecessary.

## Do not book a full-day Crete tour just to see Knossos

There are plenty of excursions combining Knossos with:

* Lassithi Plateau
* Cave of Zeus
* monasteries
* traditional villages
* olive-oil stops

Some last **8–9 hours**.

Those can be perfectly good days.

But do not confuse them with the easiest way to visit Knossos.

One current Viator itinerary spends only around **one hour at Knossos** inside an 8–9 hour day.

That tells you exactly what the product is:

a Crete sightseeing circuit that includes Knossos.

Not a Knossos-focused visit.

If the palace is your priority, I would rather give it 1.5–2 hours and then see the archaeological museum.

## Bus vs taxi

This is mostly a convenience decision.

### Choose the bus if…

You are in central Heraklion.

You are travelling alone or as a couple.

You want the cheapest option.

You do not mind a 20-minute public-transport ride.

### Choose taxi if…

Several people can share the cost.

You want door-to-door transport.

Walking to or waiting for the bus is inconvenient.

You are working around a tight schedule.

The difference in journey time is small.

The difference is comfort.

## Bus + guided tour vs organized transfer tour

This is the more interesting comparison.

### Bus + guide

You control the schedule.

Transport costs very little.

You pay mainly for historical interpretation.

This would be my default for an interested first-time visitor staying in Heraklion.

### Organized transfer tour

You remove the logistics.

The operator may collect you from your hotel or resort.

This becomes much more useful if you are **not actually staying in Heraklion city**.

That distinction matters.

## Staying in Hersonissos, Malia or another resort is different

The title of this article says **from Heraklion** for a reason.

If your hotel is in:

* Hersonissos
* Stalida
* Malia
* Gouves
* Agia Pelagia

then your transport problem changes.

Some organized Knossos tours collect travellers from these resort areas and bring them back afterward.

Suddenly a tour is not competing with a 20-minute city bus.

It is competing with:

**regional transport → Heraklion → Line 2 → Knossos → repeat everything in reverse.**

In that situation, hotel pickup can be worth paying for.

## Cruise passengers are another special case

If your ship is in Heraklion for a limited number of hours, predictability matters more.

Knossos is close enough to visit independently.

But a shore excursion can provide:

* port pickup
* guide
* transport
* structured return
* sometimes a guaranteed return-to-ship policy

That can justify the extra cost when missing the ship would be considerably more expensive than saving money on a bus.

Again, the value is not simply transportation.

It is risk reduction.

## Booking trap #1: assuming admission is included

Always check.

Current Knossos products vary.

Some include the €20 ticket.

Some list it as an extra.

Some tours to Lassithi and Knossos advertise a guide and transfer while still charging the palace admission separately.

Compare **total cost**, not headline tour price.

## Booking trap #2: paying for eight hours when you wanted two

Knossos itself does not require an 8–9 hour excursion.

If a tour lasts all day, look at everything else on the itinerary.

If those extra places excite you, great.

If you only wanted Knossos, you are buying a lot of transportation you did not need.

## Booking trap #3: confusing a guide with a tour leader

For an archaeological site like Knossos, I would specifically look for a **licensed guide**.

A tour leader who accompanies a bus through Crete is not necessarily the person legally or professionally qualified to conduct the archaeological-site tour.

Check the product wording.

## Booking trap #4: forgetting the museum

If you enjoy Knossos but skip the Heraklion Archaeological Museum entirely, you miss a major part of the story.

This does not mean everybody needs a guided museum tour.

You can visit independently.

But I would at least consider leaving space for it on the same day.

## Booking trap #5: arriving at midday in summer

Knossos has exposed areas and limited shade.

July and August can be hot and crowded.

If I were travelling independently in summer, one of the biggest advantages of the bus would be the ability to go early.

The official summer opening starts at **08:00**.

That is a better feature than any tour title containing the words “premium access”.

## Which would I choose?

### Solo traveller staying in central Heraklion

**Bus.**

Then either explore independently or join a small-group guide at the site.

### Couple interested in history

**Bus + small-group licensed guide.**

Probably the best balance of price and understanding.

### Family of four

Compare taxi with four individual bus fares.

The bus will still be cheaper, but a taxi may be worth the convenience.

### History enthusiast

**Knossos + Archaeological Museum.**

A guide becomes much easier to justify.

### Staying in Hersonissos or Malia

Look seriously at an organized pickup tour.

The transport advantage is now real.

### Cruise passenger

Taxi/private or a well-structured shore excursion may be worth paying for because time certainty matters.

### I just want to see the famous red columns and Minotaur place

Bus + official ticket.

You do not need to turn it into a €100 excursion.

## Dan's recommendation

Knossos is a good example of how travel booking sites can make a simple problem look expensive.

From central Heraklion, the palace is about twenty minutes away on an ordinary city bus.

So I would not buy a tour just because I was worried about getting there.

I would spend money only when it buys something useful:

**a licensed guide**

**hotel pickup from farther away**

**a museum combination**

**private flexibility**

or

**cruise-ship timing certainty.**

For a first visit from central Heraklion, my own comparison would start with:

**Line 2 bus + a good small-group guide at Knossos.**

Cheap transportation.

Money spent where it actually changes the experience.

And if you prefer exploring ancient sites without a guide, the answer becomes even simpler:

**take the bus.**

*Some links on this page are affiliate links. If you book through them, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.*

**Checked: 1 November 2026.**

title: Knossos Palace From Heraklion: Bus, Tour or Taxi?
